html:
The military and civil provinces of the Byzantine Empire, called themes, set up in Anatolia from the mid 600s after the loss of Syria and Egypt to the Arabs.

When the field armies retreated from the east after the Yarmuk, they were settled in Anatolia, each in its own region. The first themes took the names of these armies: the Anatolikon, the Armeniakon, the Opsikion, and later the Thrakesion. Each was run by a general, the strategos, who held both military and civil power. Over time soldiers were supported by family lands that carried a duty of service, so the empire could keep an army without enough cash to pay it.

Exactly when and how the system began is debated, but it let the empire survive a century of Arab raids and sieges. Emperors such as Leo III rose from theme commands. The themes spread to the Balkans and the islands. From the 11th century, with paid armies and land grants called pronoia taking over, the system faded, a weakness exposed at Manzikert in 1071.
sum: The military and civil provinces of the Byzantine Empire, called themes, set up in Anatolia from the mid 600s after the loss of Syria and Egypt to the Arabs.
